extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary schools, postsecondary institutions, other educational entities), Title IX coordinators, investigators, decisionmakers, school administrators, and legal counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing grievance procedures to resolve complaints of sex discrimination (including sex-based harassment) under Title IX consistent with the Department of Education's final regulations and constitutional due process principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with constitutional due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must comport with due process where constitutional protections apply (e.g., public postsecondary institutions are subject to procedural due process), and nothing in the regulations requires a recipient to restrict constitutional rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department does not intend to, and Title IX does not require, different procedural standards for public and private recipients; as an agency it is precluded from administering Title IX in a way that would require a recipient to deny constitutional due process rights (citing §106.6(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Mathews v. Eldridge factors to determine what process is due
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Mathews balancing test — (A) the private interest affected; (B) the risk of erroneous deprivation of that interest through the procedures used; and (C) the governmental interest at stake — in deciding what procedural protections are required in a particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate these three factors to determine required procedural protections; the Department concludes §§106.45 and 106.46 satisfy the Mathews factors for Title IX grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of multiple private interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must take into account that both complainants and respondents have important private interests (e.g., educational enrollment, reputation, liberty/property interests) that must be weighed in the Mathews analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that when more than one private party's interests are implicated, both must be considered (citing Brock v. Roadway Exp., Inc.). Procedures should not privilege one party's interests at the expense of the other's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must be afforded timely notice of the charges and an opportunity to review evidence and present their side of the story before any deprivation of education/employment-related interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reiterates that procedures resolving sex discrimination allegations must provide notice and an opportunity to be heard; the final regulations' framework allows a public recipient to meet constitutional due process requirements (citing Goss).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor procedures to context and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must be tailored to the unique settings and rights implicated by allegations of sex discrimination to decrease the likelihood of erroneous decisions and produce reliable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary function of legal process is to minimize erroneous decisions; courts assess the relative reliability of procedures and substitute procedures, weighing how much additional safeguards improve reliability versus their costs (citing Mackey v. Montrym and Walters v. NARST). The final regs are designed to be proportionate to the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh marginal gains versus societal/administrative costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering additional procedural safeguards, evaluate whether marginal gains in accuracy or reliability are outweighed by societal costs, including administrative efficiency and potential deterrence of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if additional procedures could improve reliability, due process does not require them if their marginal benefit is outweighed by societal costs (e.g., discouraging complainants). Administrative efficiency is a legitimate consideration (citing Walters; Dixon v. Love).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on bias and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person designated as a Title IX Coordinator, investigator, decisionmaker, or facilitator of informal resolution must not have a conflict of interest or bias against complainants or respondents generally or an individual party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations explicitly require no conflict of interest or bias (§106.45(b)(2); §106.46(a); §106.46(k)(4)). Bias is an express ground for appeal from a dismissal or a determination (§§106.45(d)(3), 106.46(i)(1)(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that respondent is not responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance procedures must include a presumption that the respondent is not responsible for the alleged sex discrimination until a determination is made at the conclusion of the recipient's grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is required by the final regulations (§106.45(b)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment and objective evaluation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure equitable treatment of the parties and apply standards for objective evaluation of relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence; determinations must not be reached before the conclusion of the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific provisions require equitable treatment, address conflict of interest and bias, set standards for objective evidence evaluation, and bar premature determinations (see §106.45(b)(1), (2), (6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections, exclusion of impermissible evidence/questions, and control of disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must take reasonable steps to protect parties' privacy, exclude certain types of evidence and questions as impermissible, and regulate or prevent unauthorized disclosure of information related to alleged sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include protecting parties' privacy (§106.45(b)(5), (7)), excluding impermissible evidence/questions, and taking steps to prevent and address unauthorized disclosure (§106.45(f)(4)(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure respondents (and complainants) have access to supportive measures to mitigate harms while protecting their rights and access to educational programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations require provision of supportive measures (see §§106.44(f)(1)(ii), (g), 106.45(l)(1)). Supportive measures are part of the Title IX Coordinator's obligations upon notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator duties upon notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon being notified of conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination, a Title IX Coordinator must take certain actions, including offering and coordinating supportive measures and, when available and appropriate, offering informal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps aim to mitigate deterrent effects and assist parties; see §§106.44(f)(1)(ii), (f)(1)(iv), (g), (k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness and reasonable timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must be conducted promptly; recipients may designate reasonable timeframes for their procedures provided they are 'reasonably prompt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to set timeframes as long as they are reasonably prompt (§106.45(b)(4)). The Department modified prior rules to address concerns about lengthy procedures, especially for younger students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in structuring procedures and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain significant flexibility in structuring procedures: they may use their own employees or contractors as investigators/decisionmakers, use a single decisionmaker or a panel, determine remedies/sanctions, offer informal resolution, and formulate appeal procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations explicitly preserve recipient discretion on staffing and procedural choices (§§106.8(a)(2), 106.45(b)(2), 106.45(k), 106.45(h)(3)-(4), 106.45(i), 106.46(i)). This flexibility is balanced against standardized enforcement goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requiring grievance procedures to mimic criminal/civil judicial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures are not required to replicate criminal or civil court procedures; requirements that appeared quasi-judicial in prior rules (e.g., mandatory live hearing, ban on single-investigator model) have been relaxed to allow non-attorneys to implement fair procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department removed prescriptive 2020 amendment requirements (e.g., mandatory live hearing, prohibition on single-investigator) and allows postsecondary institutions discretion to assess credibility via a live hearing or another live questioning process (§§106.46(f)-(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to take emergency actions to protect the educational environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may remove a respondent from an education program or activity on an emergency basis or place an employee respondent on administrative leave during the pendency of grievance procedures when warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations permit emergency removals (§106.44(h)) and administrative leave for employees (§106.44(i)), so long as required procedural safeguards are observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability rules: separate treatment for student-involved sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution must apply §106.45 to complaints of sex discrimination generally (including employee-to-employee harassment) but must apply §106.46 for sex-based harassment complaints that involve a student party (including where an employee is the other party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bifurcation reflects differences in legal relationships (e.g., Title VII applies to employees but not students) and the Department's view that additional protections in §106.46 are appropriate for student parties (see §106.46(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution options
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may offer and facilitate informal resolution processes, and Title IX Coordinators should offer informal resolution when available and appropriate to the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution is discretionary but must be offered consistent with §§106.44(k) and related provisions; safeguards and facilitator impartiality are required (see §106.46(k)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals must include bias and other specified bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals procedures must include grounds for appeal such as bias and other reasons specified in the regulations (e.g., specified bases for appeals from dismissals or determinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations explicitly provide bias as a ground for appeal (§§106.45(d)(3), 106.46(i)(1)(iii)). Recipients must formulate appeals consistent with §§106.45(i) and 106.46(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and safeguards to prevent biased procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must implement appropriate training and other safeguards designed to prevent biased procedures and disproportionate impacts on respondents from diverse backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations build on prior provisions requiring training to seek to prevent bias (see §106.8(d)(2)(iii), (3) and the discussion of anti-bias provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory scope and no safe-harbor exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX grievance procedure obligations apply to all recipients of Federal financial assistance (not limited to Clery-covered entities); the Department will not create a 'safe harbor' exemption based on Clery Act reporting or other metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations apply broadly (elementary/secondary schools, SEAs, libraries, museums, etc.). Religious exemptions remain statutory and under Congressional authority (20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(3)). The Department declines to permit safe-harbor exemptions for administrative burden reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: fair, transparent, reliable determinations and remedies to restore access
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall purpose of grievance procedures is to reach fair, transparent, and reliable determinations so the recipient can address sex discrimination and ensure complainants receive remedies designed to restore or preserve equal access to the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations do not prescribe particular sanctions but focus on procedural features that promote accurate outcomes and appropriate remedies (§106.45(h)(3)-(4)). The Department maintains that these benefits justify procedural burdens.
